turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oof. That's such a specific, tender kind of stuck — because it's not "do I want to be there," it's "how do I be fully there as myself."

Can I ask what the dread is actually made of? Because I'm hearing a few possible things tangled together. There's the practical — dancing on an empty stomach, sangeet timings that probably start way after Maghrib anyway, energy levels. And then there's the other layer: a cocktail night, during Ramzan, and you being the one person in the room navigating something everyone else isn't. That can feel lonely even when you're surrounded by people who love you.

The practical bits might be more workable than they feel right now. Sangeets rarely kick off before 8-9pm — you'd have broken your fast by then. Rehearsals are the trickier part, and honestly, a "let's do practice sessions post-iftar" conversation with Shreya might solve more than you'd expect.

But the cocktail night is its own thing, and you're allowed to do that one differently. Show up for an hour, be there for her, leave when it stops feeling okay. That's not being a bad co-director.

Has she asked how any of this lands for you? Or is she just in full bridal tunnel vision?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

That line — "both sides love me and neither gets it" — that's the whole thing, isn't it. It'd be so much easier if someone were being unkind. Then you'd know where to stand. Instead you're doing the exhausting work of translating between two people who both think they're protecting you.

And Shreya's line — I believe she meant it as the sweetest thing she could offer. "I'll feed you myself." She thinks she's offering care. She doesn't realise she's asking you to hand over something that isn't hers to hold. You don't have to be angry at her to be hurt by it.

Here's the thing though — she probably *can* get it, if you tell her plainly. Not defensively, just: "Shreya, I'm not skipping the fast. That part's not negotiable. What I need is help figuring out how I do everything else *around* it." She's known you since you were fifteen. Give her the chance to rise to it — most people do, when you stop softening the ask.

Ammi's harder, because it's not really about logistics for her. Is it more the cocktail-night part, or the whole thing?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

I get why it's tempting. It's not terrible — it's the fantasy of a tired person who's been carrying too much translation work. That part makes complete sense.

But I don't think it'd work the way you're hoping. Not because you'd get caught — because you'd lose her wedding. The one you've been co-directing since you were fifteen. You'd trade ten awkward conversations for a grief that'd sit in your chest for years, and Shreya would be missing her person on the biggest day of her life without knowing why. That's a heavy thing to hand yourself just to avoid some aunties.

And here's what I want to push on: the ten explanations aren't actually yours to give. You don't owe any aunty a reason. "I'm fasting" is a complete sentence. "No thanks" while holding a glass of juice is a complete sentence. Most of them won't even notice — people at weddings are far more absorbed in themselves than we imagine.

The exhaustion you're feeling isn't really about the logistics. It's from bracing for a hundred imagined conversations. That's a much bigger weight than the actual night will be.

What if you gave yourself permission to be a *smaller* presence than co-director? Opening dance with Shreya, yes. Skip the cocktail night or drop in for twenty minutes. Let someone else manage the playlist crisis. You've been holding the whole production — you're allowed to just be her friend that week.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That's the sentence underneath everything else, isn't it. Not logistics — legacy. Both things are permanent records, and you're terrified of being the smudge in one of them.

But I want to offer you something: I don't think this collision is a test you pass or fail. Eighteen years of friendship isn't fragile enough to dent from one week of complicated scheduling. And your Ramzan isn't a report card either — a Ramzan where you kept your fasts *and* danced with your best friend at her sangeet after iftar isn't a compromised Ramzan. It might be one of the ones you remember most fondly. Joy isn't a deduction.

The sad-story version only happens if you disappear. That's the one that leaves a real hole in both albums.

You've spent this whole conversation trying to protect everyone — Shreya's happiness, Ammi's peace, your deen. You're allowed to be a person in this too, not just the rope. Tell Shreya the truth, let her love you through it, dance the opening number with an empty stomach and a full heart, and go home early if you want to.

Eighteen years. She'll remember you were there. Not what you were holding.
